query: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has high strength at room temperature and elevated temperature but a relatively high density of 10.21 g cm−3. What single intervention could reduce its density without sacrificing its mechanical properties at room temperature and at elevated temperatures, including approximately 1000 °C? State the proposed intervention and mechanism, predict directional changes relative to as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, define the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, identify supporting prior evidence, and propose an experiment and rejection criterion that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The introduction of a small amount of boron (B) into the HfMoTaTiZr alloy through powder metallurgy processing can reduce its density without sacrificing its mechanical properties at room temperature and elevated temperatures.
generation.intervention: Addition of a small amount of boron (B) into the HfMoTaTiZr alloy through powder metallurgy processing
generation.conditions: Processing conditions: powder metallurgy; Temperature range: room temperature to 1000 °C
generation.mechanism: The addition of boron can lead to the formation of boride precipitates, which can refine the grain structure and improve the strength of the alloy while reducing its density due to the lower atomic mass of boron compared to the other elements in the alloy.
generation.predicted_outcome: Reduced density, improved strength, and maintained mechanical properties at room temperature and elevated temperatures
generation.baseline: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy with a density of 10.21 g cm−3
generation.boundary: Temperature range: room temperature to 1000 °C; Loading conditions: tensile and compressive loading
generation.uncertainty: The optimal amount of boron addition and the resulting microstructure are uncertain and require further investigation

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare HfMoTaTiZr alloys with varying amounts of boron addition (0, 0.1, 0.5, 1.0 wt%) through powder metallurgy processing. Test the density, tensile strength, and compressive strength of the alloys at room temperature and 1000 °C.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the addition of boron does not result in a reduction in density or a significant decrease in mechanical properties at room temperature or 1000 °C, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are a relatively new class of multicomponent materials that are based on several refractory metals, but may also contain other, generally low density, elements and typically have a body centered cubic (BCC) crystal structure [1] – [3] . These alloys have recently received much attention because of their attractive combination of properties not achievable by other classes of metallic alloys. For example, the first two RHEAs, NbMoTaW and NbMoTaVW, showed weak temperature dependence of yield strength in the temperature range from 600 °C to 1600 °C, with yield strength above 400 MPa at 1600 °C [4] , [5] . Unfortunately, these two alloys had high density (>12 g/cm 3 ) and further developments aimed at reducing the alloy density while keeping superior high-temperature properties. In the second generation RHEAs, high-density Ta and W were replaced with lower density refractory elements, such as Cr, Mo, Nb, V and Zr, and low density Al and Ti were added [6] – [13] . Recently the concept of high-entropy alloys (HEAs), consisting of four or more principle metallic elements in equiatomic or near-equiatomic ratios, has attracted considerable interest owing to its tendency to form solid solution with outstanding mechanical and functional properties [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. By introducing refractory elements including group IV (Ti, Zr, and Hf), V (V, Nb, and Ta), and VI (Cr, Mo, and W) in HEAs, the developed refractory HEAs (RHEAs) possess high melting temperature, outstanding strength and hardness, high thermal stability, and softening resistance at elevated temperatures, which opens up the possibilities of the alloy developments satisfying structural demands at high temperature.

Since the first WMoTaNb RHEA was reported in 2010, many literatures have been focused on the preparation methods and mechanical properties of RHEAs [ [7] , [8] ]. For example, the BCC WMoTaNb and WMoTaNbV HEAs maintained yield strength of 405 and 477 MPa at 1600 °C respectively, which were much higher than that of Inconel 718 and Haynes 230 [ [9] ].
